## How this review was done

I read all six files — three lectures and three practicals, about 9,900
lines — and ran code where a claim could be checked rather than taken on
trust. Every number quoted below was produced by running something, not
read off a slide. Where I say a link or a path is broken, I checked it.

The headline: **this is a strong, unusually honest three-lecture series
with a real case study and a genuine argument running through it.** Most
of what follows is small corrections and one substantial recommendation
about grouping factors. The Python problem in Volume 3 turns out to be
solvable without changing packages, and that is in [its own
section](#the-python-mixed-models-problem).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What is good — and worth protecting

These are the things I would not change, because they are what makes the
series work.

**The recipe framing earns its keep.** "Step 1 — Ingredients" spends an
entire third of Volume 1 on EDA before a model is fitted, and the slide
that says *the process of exploring your data should take much longer
than the modelling at the end* is the single most useful sentence in the
series. Most regression teaching inverts this.

**The case study has real stakes.** Brighton and Hove Council made an
actual admissions policy decision on the basis of Gorard's work, and the
lectures are explicitly an argument about whether the evidence supports
it. Students are not modelling a toy dataset; they are auditing a live
policy. The "**So the council was right? Well, not quite...**" beat in
Volume 1 is the moment the series stops being a stats course.

**"A regression model is nothing more than a description of a scatter
plot."** This is the right first sentence about regression and it is
followed properly — line of best fit, residuals, R², slope and intercept
all built visually from the same plot before any algebra appears.

**The degrees-of-freedom sequence is excellent.** Building from 2 points
to 3 to 4 to 5, showing the line pivoting, makes "degrees of freedom" a
thing you can see rather than a number in an output. I have not seen it
taught this way elsewhere and it works.

**The deliberate failure in Volume 1.** Fitting on 10 Brighton schools,
getting a satisfying R² of 0.69, and then showing that three *plausible*
policy changes flatten the relationship to nothing — and that the model
goes statistically insignificant — is the best teaching in the series. It
makes overfitting visceral instead of abstract.

**The diagnostics scoreboard** carried from Volume 1 into Volume 2, with
the emoji going from 😭 to 😎 as each assumption gets addressed, gives the
two lectures a spine. Students always know where they are.

**The VIF intuition.** *"If two variables are highly correlated and both
appear to affect the outcome, the model makes an arbitrary split. Small
changes in the data could make the split go either way — thus inflating
the variance."* That is the clearest one-paragraph explanation of
multicollinearity I have read in a course.

**"ALWAYS MAP YOUR RESIDUALS IF MODELLING SPATIAL DATA"**, with the
London effect visible on the map, is a lesson that will outlive the
course.

**The confounding section quantifies itself.** Showing the disadvantage
coefficient shrink from −0.21 to −0.11 (44.5%) while absence shrinks from
−0.54 to −0.41 (24.6%), and concluding that disadvantage is *almost
twice* as biased by the omission, is exactly the right level of rigour.

**The Gabber/Hakken mediation example** is genuinely funny and will be
remembered. Keep it.

**Volume 3's shrinkage treatment** — that groups with few observations
get pulled toward the global mean, and that this is a *feature* which
avoids overfitting to small groups — is well judged, and the paired
visualisations do real work.

## Things that are wrong and should be fixed

### 1. The p-value is defined correctly and then immediately inverted {#p-value}

Volume 1 gets it right first:

> The $P$-value — probability of observing a t-value as extreme as the one
> calculated **if there were no relationship** between the independent and
> the dependent variable

and then, on the same slide:

> A small $P$-value (typically $p$ \< 0.05) indicates **\<5% chance that
> $X$ is not really explaining variation in $Y$**

and on the next slide:

> $P$ \<0.001 = \<0.1% $P$-robability that 62.3 **occurred by random
> chance**

The second and third statements are the inverse-probability fallacy —
they say $P(\text{no relationship} \mid \text{data})$ when the p-value is
$P(\text{data} \mid \text{no relationship})$. This is *the* most common
misconception about p-values, students will carry it into their
dissertations, and it is being stated here immediately after the correct
definition.

**Suggested fix** — keep the first definition and rephrase the others as:

> A small p-value means data like ours would be **surprising** if there
> were really no relationship. It does not tell us the probability that
> there is no relationship — for that you would need to know how likely a
> relationship was before you looked.

### 2. The standard-error interval is a 68% interval presented as if it were the interval

> SE of 0.15 for the estimate of −0.63 means the change could vary between
> **−0.48 and −0.78**

That is estimate ± 1 SE, which is roughly a 68% interval. The
conventional 95% interval is ±1.96 SE, i.e. **−0.34 to −0.92** — nearly
twice as wide, and a much more honest picture of the uncertainty in a
model with 8 degrees of freedom. Either widen it or say explicitly that
this is a one-standard-error range.

### 3. Comparing predictor "importance" by t-value

Both Volume 1 and Volume 2 use t-values to rank predictors:

> t-values indicate that the % Overall Absence variable (−50.49) has a
> **stronger effect** than the % Disadvantaged Students variable (−31.16)

A t-value is $\hat\beta/\text{SE}$, so it confounds effect size with
precision. With n ≈ 3,000 both are overwhelmingly significant and the
ratio mostly reflects how well each coefficient is pinned down, not how
much each matters.

**There is a better move available, and the lecture has already set it
up.** Both variables are logged, so their coefficients are
**elasticities** and *are* directly comparable: a 1% rise in absence is
associated with a 0.41% fall in Attainment 8, against 0.11% for
disadvantage. That is a cleaner comparison than the t-values, it needs no
caveat, and it reinforces the elasticity idea introduced a few slides
earlier.

### 4. Ofsted rating is the wrong grouping factor for Volume 3 {#grouping}

This is the one substantive recommendation in this review.

Volume 3 uses `OFSTEDRATING` as the random effect throughout — the null
model, the ICC, the random-intercept model and the random-slope model.
There are two problems.

**It has too few groups, and two are tiny.** Counting from the data:

| Ofsted rating | Schools |
|---------------|---------|
| Good | 2,235 |
| Outstanding | 468 |
| Requires improvement | 407 |
| Serious Weaknesses | **44** |
| Special Measures | **32** |

Five groups is at the very bottom of what will support a between-group
variance estimate — the usual guidance is a minimum of five and a
preference for considerably more — and two of them are small enough that
their intercepts are almost entirely shrinkage. The lecture teaches
shrinkage beautifully and then picks a grouping factor where shrinkage
does nearly all the work.

**And it is close to circular.** An Ofsted rating is in part a *judgement
about attainment*. Modelling attainment as clustered within Ofsted rating
asks how much of the variation in attainment is explained by a grading of
attainment. This is precisely the circularity the new GLM lecture (Vol 4)
now warns about in its closing slides, where Progress 8 turns out to be
something inspectors read before they visit.

**What to use instead.** The same data has much better candidates:

| Grouping factor | Groups | Comment |
|-----------------|--------|---------|
| `LANAME` (local authority) | **152** | Genuine nesting, policy-relevant, matches the Brighton framing |
| DfE region | **25** | Good higher level; picks up the London effect from Vol 2 |
| `OFSTEDRATING` | 5 | Currently used |

Local authority is the natural choice: it is a real administrative
hierarchy, it has 152 groups, it connects directly to the Brighton and
Hove question the series opens with, and `(1 | region/LANAME)` gives a
genuine three-level model to demonstrate nesting properly.

I fitted both to check this is not just theory. With
`log(ATT8) ~ log(FSM)`:

| Model | Between-group variance | Residual variance |
|-------|------------------------|-------------------|
| `(1 \| region/LANAME)` | region 0.00669, LA-within-region 0.00261 | 0.01354 |
| `(1 \| OFSTEDRATING) + (1 \| LANAME)` | Ofsted 0.01206, LA 0.00593 | 0.01101 |

Both fit fine. The nested version is the one that tells a story about
geography and policy; the Ofsted version tells a story about a grading
system grading itself.

**If you want to keep Ofsted**, the honest framing is to use it as a
*second, crossed* random effect alongside local authority and say out
loud why it is a strange one — which is a good discussion and now ties
directly into Vol 4.

### 5. A small but misleading sentence about shrinkage

> Remember: Higher variance = Higher uncertainty, so **higher variance
> groups have less weight** in the model

What determines how much a group is shrunk is the *sampling variance of
that group's mean* — roughly $\sigma^2/n_j$ — so it is mostly about
**group size**. As written it reads as though the between-group variance
$\sigma^2_{\text{group}}$ is what pulls a group in, which is the opposite:
a large between-group variance means groups are shrunk *less*. Suggest:

> Groups with **few observations** have unreliable means, so they get
> pulled furthest toward the global average.

### 6. The equations label a variable the models do not use

Volume 2 writes:

$$\log(\text{Attainment8}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\log(\text{PctDisadvantage}) + \beta_2\log(\text{PctPersistentAbsence}) + \epsilon$$

and the interaction equations use `PctPersistentAbsence` too. But the
models, the code and the interpretation all use `PERCTOT`, which is
**overall absence**, not persistent absence — `PPERSABS10` is the
persistent-absence variable and is not in these models. The slides'
prose says "overall absence" correctly while the maths above it says
something else. Rename to `PctOverallAbsence` throughout.

## The Python mixed-models problem {#the-python-mixed-models-problem}

**Short answer: statsmodels can do it, including the crossed and nested
random effects you got stuck on. You do not need to change packages.**

You said you could not find Python equivalents for the R code. The place
this bites is the Final Task in Volume 3's practical, which asks students
to extend the model with

``` r
lmer(log(ATT8SCR) ~ ... + (1 | OFSTEDRATING) + (1 | gor_name/LANAME), data = ...)
```

That is **two grouping factors, one of them nested**. `statsmodels`'
`MixedLM` takes a single `groups=` argument, so the obvious translation
has nowhere to put the second factor — which I assume is exactly where
you stopped.

The way through is `vc_formula` (variance components), which is
documented but not at all obvious. Two idioms cover everything in the
practical.

### Nested random effects — `(1 | region/LA)`

Put the **top** level in `groups` and the **lower** level in
`vc_formula`. Note `re_formula="1"` is required: without it statsmodels
silently drops the group-level intercept when `vc_formula` is present,
which is a trap worth knowing about.

``` python
m = smf.mixedlm("log_ATT8 ~ log_FSM",
                data=d,
                groups=d["region_name"],
                re_formula="1",                          # region intercept
                vc_formula={"LA": "0 + C(LANAME)"}       # LA within region
               ).fit()
```

### Crossed random effects — `(1 | OFSTEDRATING) + (1 | LANAME)`

There is no group hierarchy, so put *everything* in `vc_formula` and give
`groups` a constant column:

``` python
d["one"] = 1
m = smf.mixedlm("log_ATT8 ~ log_FSM",
                data=d,
                groups=d["one"],                         # one group: all rows
                re_formula="0",                          # no group intercept
                vc_formula={"ofsted": "0 + C(OFSTEDRATING)",
                            "la":     "0 + C(LANAME)"}
               ).fit()
```

### It gives the same answers as lme4

I ran both against `lmer` on 3,186 schools. These are the actual outputs:

**Nested, `(1 | region/LANAME)`**

| Component | lme4 | statsmodels |
|---------------------|-----------|-------------|
| region variance | 0.006688 | 0.006687 |
| LA within region | 0.002605 | 0.002605 |
| residual | 0.013538 | 0.013538 |
| intercept | 4.65677 | 4.65676 |
| slope | −0.26297 | −0.26297 |

**Crossed, `(1 | OFSTEDRATING) + (1 | LANAME)`**

| Component | lme4 | statsmodels |
|---------------------|-----------|-------------|
| LANAME variance | 0.005934 | 0.005933 |
| OFSTED variance | 0.012058 | 0.012036 |
| residual | 0.011010 | 0.011010 |
| intercept | 4.49769 | 4.49769 |
| slope | −0.22686 | −0.22686 |

Agreement to four or five decimal places, and the crossed model fits in
**0.9 seconds**. Two notes for the practical: statsmodels orders the
variance components **alphabetically** in the output (`la` before
`ofsted`), regardless of dictionary order; and it reports **variances**
where `lmer`'s default print shows variance *and* standard deviation.

### Why not pymer4

You offered to refactor around `pymer4`, and I tested it properly before
answering. It does work on this machine, but the cost is high:

-   `pip install pymer4` alone is not enough — its dependency metadata is
    incomplete, and it additionally needs `polars`, `rpy2` and
    `great_tables` installed by hand
-   `rpy2` needs `R_HOME` set **and** `R_HOME/bin/x64` added to the DLL
    search path on Windows, or R's `stats.dll` fails to load
-   it has to be run with the project's `renv` profile disabled, or R
    exhausts its cons memory on startup
-   it then failed on an R-side version conflict (`rlang` 1.1.6 installed,
    ≥ 1.1.7 required)

**And the decisive objection:** `pymer4` is a wrapper around R's `lme4`
via `rpy2`. Every student would need a working R installation *and* a
consistent R package library *and* the Windows DLL path set — which
defeats the purpose of offering a Python route at all. The students most
likely to choose the Python tab are precisely those least likely to have
a working R toolchain.

I installed all of it to test, confirmed the above, and then removed
`pymer4`, `rpy2`, `polars`, `great_tables` and `tzlocal` again so the
virtual environment still matches `requirements.txt`.

## Structural observations

### Python coverage collapses exactly where it is needed most

Counting code chunks by language:

| Practical | R chunks | Python chunks | Parity |
|---------------------------|----------|---------------|--------|
| Vol 1 — regression | 25 | 22 | **88%** |
| Vol 2 — multiple regression | 17 | 9 | **53%** |
| Vol 3 — multilevel | 21 | 11 | **52%** |

A student who picks the Python tab gets a good experience in week one and
is increasingly abandoned thereafter. Given that the fix above removes the
main technical blocker in Vol 3, closing this gap is now mostly
transcription work rather than research.

### A 65 MB download on a personal Dropbox link

The Volume 3 lecture reads `edubasealldata20241003.csv` from a Dropbox
share. I checked: it is live and returns **64.8 MB**. That is a single
point of failure owned by one person's account, fetched on every render,
and if a class of students hits it at once a free Dropbox account can be
rate-limited. Worth moving into `sessions/data/` with the rest, or
reducing to just the columns the lecture uses.

### Volume 3 switches outcome variable mid-lecture

The null-model section says it is partitioning the variance in **Progress
8 (P8MEA)**, but the worked models and the practical use **Attainment 8
(ATT8SCR)**. Pick one. Progress 8 is arguably the better choice for a
multilevel treatment since it is already adjusted for intake, but
whichever you choose it should be consistent.

### Volume 3 carries a lot of hidden code

`multilevel_regression_lecture.qmd` has 5 chunks set `eval: false` and 8
set `include: false`; the practical has 3 and 7. Some of that is
deliberate, but several of the `include: false` chunks in the practical's
Final Task are substantial models whose output never appears. Worth a pass
to work out which are scaffolding and which are dead.

### Overlap with the new GLM lecture

Vol 4 now covers three things these lectures also touch, and the
duplication is worth resolving deliberately rather than by accident:

-   **Overfitting** — Vol 1 does it with the three Brighton schools, Vol 4
    with an interpolating spline. Both are good and they are complementary;
    a one-line cross-reference in each direction would help.
-   **Comparing against a baseline** — Vol 4 makes this a rule. Vols 1–3
    never compare a model against doing nothing, which would be a natural
    addition to the Vol 2 evaluation task.
-   **Circularity of the predictors** — Vol 4 closes on it. As noted
    [above](#grouping), Vol 3's choice of grouping factor is an unflagged
    instance of the same problem, and connecting the two would strengthen
    both.

**Before the sessions run**

2.  Fix the p-value wording ([§1](#p-value)) — this is the one that does
    lasting damage
3.  Fix the typos in slide titles and the `::sunglasses::` emoji

**Worth doing properly**

4.  Switch Vol 3's grouping factor to local authority, or add it alongside
    Ofsted and discuss why Ofsted is a strange choice ([§4](#grouping))
5.  Add the Python mixed-model code above to the Vol 3 practical and close
    the Final Task gap
6.  Rename `PctPersistentAbsence` to `PctOverallAbsence` in the Vol 2
    equations
7.  Replace the t-value "importance" comparison with the elasticity
    comparison

**When there is time**

8.  Bring Python parity in Vols 2 and 3 up toward Vol 1's level
9.  Move the 65 MB Dropbox file into the repo's own data folder
10. Settle on Progress 8 or Attainment 8 in Vol 3
11. Audit the `include: false` chunks
12. Add cross-references to and from Vol 4

## One thing I would not change

The series takes a position. It opens with a council that has made a
policy decision, builds a model that appears to support it, and then
spends two and a half lectures showing why the first answer was too
simple — small samples, confounding, omitted geography, clustered
errors — without ever concluding that the council was simply wrong. That
argumentative spine is rare in quantitative methods teaching and it is
what will make students remember the statistics. Everything above is in
service of it.
